name: Cryptic crossword No 24,003
preamble: Solutions to the three starred clues are literally identical and not further defined

clue.text: *Lace reworked in suit by couple having love and money without sex appeal

indicators.note: material that has been worked is kneaded and reshaped, so the letters are remade into a fresh order
one thing placed inside another is held there, so this piece goes within the next
used in its old sense of outside, so the second piece wraps around the first

blocks.note: LACE plus the RE that begins the next word, rearranged
a suit at law is an action
a duet is a pair of performers
love is nil in tennis, shaped like the letter O
gravy is slang for easy money
'it' was the 1920s word for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A couple in lace-trimmed suits, rich and in love but somehow unappealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder steals RE from 'reworked', leaving 'worked' as the signal. As a starred clue it has no definition: its answer is abbreviated g, like the other two starred answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Physicists write the constant rate at which falling bodies speed up near the Earth as small g, making it identical to the other starred solutions.

clue.text: Bill gets skin disease, reportedly from sea anemone

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
tinea is ringworm, a fungal skin infection

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill catches a rash, supposedly from handling a sea anemone.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill sounds like a person, but it is an account. 'Reportedly' hedges because the usual spelling of the anemone is actinia; this is a variant.
explanation.definitionFit: Actinea is a variant name for a sea anemone, after the genus Actinia of soft-bodied marine animals.

clue.text: American money, very little of it, is focused

definitions.note: the definition is a verb phrase; the answer a participle

blocks.note: the cent is a US coin
having very little money puts you in the red

explanation.surface: Someone with hardly any dollars to their name is single-minded about getting more.
explanation.walkthrough: Being in the red means being overdrawn, so very little money is RED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be centred on something is to be concentrated or focused upon it.

clue.text: "Mud in your eye" coming up without a lot of speed for old dandy's curls

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means read from bottom to top
a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the tail is dropped
without in its old sense of outside, so the earlier piece goes round the later one

blocks.note: both are drinking toasts
VELOCITY with its last three letters gone

explanation.surface: A toast is raised to an old dandy and his fast-curled hair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mud in your eye' and skol are both things you say when raising a glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovelocks were long curling locks worn by fashionable seventeenth-century men, so an old dandy wore them.

clue.text: Tree sharing name with primate

blocks.note: first meaning: the mountain ash
second meaning: the given name of Dr Williams, then Archbishop of Canterbury

explanation.walkthrough: Primate looks like an ape, but here it is a senior archbishop. Rowan Williams was Primate of All England when this puzzle appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: The mountain ash bears this common name, and the Archbishop of Canterbury of the time had it as his given name.

clue.text: Illegal bowler in controversy's in the right

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: a row is a heated dispute; the 's is 'is'
THE as written plus R, the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A cricketer accused of an illegal bowling action is at the centre of a dispute, but is cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a bowler must deliver with a straight arm; one who bends and straightens the elbow is said to throw, which is illegal.
explanation.definitionFit: A chucker in cricket, whose straightened-arm delivery breaks the laws of the game, is called a thrower.

clue.text: Surprised at a mole having to do porridge

indicators.note: someone surprised is thrown off balance, so the letters are knocked into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is startled to find a mole has been given porridge to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porridge' is also British slang for a prison sentence, which colours 'having to do'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatmeal is ground oats, and the word is also used for the cooked breakfast dish made from them.

clue.text: In 26 gaga characters acquire camels etc

indicators.note: a thing set in another is held by it, so the following pieces go inside
the word's characters are taken as loose letters, free to be set in any order

blocks.note: 26 across is INTELLIGENCE, and a brain is intelligence
the four letters reordered
to acquire is to get

explanation.surface: Silly people in the know about something acquire camels and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to INTELLIGENCE, which must be turned into a synonym before it can hold anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A baggage train is the column of pack animals and carts carrying an army's supplies, of which camels are an example.

clue.text: Russian plane attaining speed in a month

indicators.note: one item inside another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: taken as written
a ton is slang for a hundred miles an hour
NOV is the calendar abbreviation for November

explanation.surface: A Russian aircraft reaches top speed over the course of a month.
explanation.walkthrough: Doing a ton is British slang for driving at a hundred miles an hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonov is the Soviet-era design bureau whose name labels a family of transport aircraft built there.

clue.text: Material beat

blocks.note: first meaning: a smooth woollen fabric
second meaning: defeated, got the better of

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a weaver's beaten cloth, but the two words are separate meanings; the second is a past tense verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The fabric is spun from long combed wool, and to have worsted someone is to have defeated them.

clue.text: See 1 across
*Commander getting information

blocks.note: a general commands an army
intelligence is gathered information, especially military

explanation.surface: An army chief receives a briefing.
explanation.walkthrough: As a starred clue it carries no definition; the two military words simply join up.
explanation.definitionFit: Psychologists label the underlying factor in mental ability with small g, so it matches the other starred solutions literally.

clue.text: Utopia in this time and place

blocks.note: the present moment
joins the two pieces
'this place' is here

explanation.surface: Paradise is to be found right here and now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' serves both time and place. Thomas More coined Utopia from Greek for 'no place'.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia literally means no place, an imagined perfect land that exists nowhere at all.

clue.text: *Old man deprived of all these years

indicators.note: to be deprived of something is to have it taken away

blocks.note: an old man may be called grandad
anno domini, the years of the present era

explanation.surface: An elderly man has been robbed of his whole lifetime.
explanation.walkthrough: AD counts every year since the birth of Christ, hence all these years. As a starred clue it has no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand, slang for a thousand pounds or dollars, is abbreviated to small g, like the other starred solutions.

clue.text: Jersey etc for primate slightly affected by smoke

indicators.note: something only slightly affected is changed a little, so just a couple of letters move

blocks.note: Jersey is one of the Channel Islands, abbreviated CI
a gorilla is a great ape, a primate

explanation.surface: An island jumper made for an ape that has been lightly singed by smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey looks like a sweater; it is the island. Only the O and A of the ape swap places, hence 'slightly'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cigarillo is a small thin cigar, and to have a smoke is to puff on one.

clue.text: Minimal clothing might be partly starred

blocks.note: surface reading: the skimpiest possible garment
setter's reading: the starred answers are each a letter of the same name, so a row of them is a string of that letter

explanation.surface: A skimpy costume worn by someone who is partly a star.
explanation.walkthrough: The three starred answers all abbreviate to the letter g, so a run of them is a string of gees; 'partly' because the garment's name is only partly that.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny garment is a narrow strip of cloth covering the groin, held by a waist cord, as worn by strippers.

clue.text: Tennessee

blocks.note: every letter of the single clue word is kept, in order

explanation.walkthrough: Araucaria gives this one away outright: clue and solution are the same word, and the joke is the solver hunting for wordplay that is not there. It may nod to Tennessee Williams, sharing a surname with the primate of 4 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue word and the solution are spelt identically, naming the southern US state and the dramatist's adopted first name.

clue.text: Ulster river in 12, not for the press

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it

blocks.note: Northern Ireland, the province often called Ulster
R is the map abbreviation for river
twelve o'clock midday, not the 12 across entry

explanation.surface: A Northern Irish river lies in some utopia, kept out of the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' looks like a cross-reference to 12 across but is the hour, noon. 'The press' is ironing, not journalism.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-iron fabric needs no pressing with a hot iron after washing, so it is never put under the press.

clue.text: Queen finds river sternutatory

blocks.note: Elizabeth Regina
the great European river

explanation.surface: The monarch discovers a river that makes her sneeze.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the Queen's royal cipher, a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rare medical words for a substance that provokes sneezing or a nasal discharge, such as snuff.

clue.text: Hide 106 balls?

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral 100, the first part of the number
a cricket over is six balls, the rest of the number

explanation.surface: A question about hiding a hundred-odd balls.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six deliveries, so 100 plus six balls is C plus OVER. The number and balls work together.
explanation.definitionFit: To hide something is to cover it, conceal it beneath something; both are verbs.

clue.text: Put Matthews in England team as winder

blocks.note: read with 'in England team', which it is split from: to cap is to pick a player for the national side
completes the phrase begun by 'Put'; it supplies no letters of its own
Sir Stanley Matthews, the great England footballer

explanation.surface: A selector picks Stanley Matthews for England as a winger.
explanation.walkthrough: The selection phrase is split around the footballer's name, so the solver must reassemble it. 'Winder' is a sly twist on winger, the position Matthews played.
explanation.definitionFit: A capstan is a revolving drum on a ship for winding in rope or cable, so it is a winder.

clue.text: Affection returned by amazingly true bird

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came
amazing things are astonishing and out of the ordinary, so the letters fall out of their usual order

blocks.note: luv is a colloquial spelling of love
taken as written

explanation.surface: Love is answered by a remarkably faithful bird.
explanation.walkthrough: Luv is the jokey British spelling of love, as in a term of endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: A vulture is a large carrion-eating raptor, a specific example of a bird.

clue.text: Playing tie near course

indicators.note: playing with something means moving it around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A match is close to a tie on the playing field.
explanation.walkthrough: Aintree, near Liverpool, is the racecourse that hosts the Grand National steeplechase.
explanation.definitionFit: A racecourse is a course, and Aintree is one of Britain's best-known examples of a horse-racing venue.

clue.text: Solver's in line for solvent

indicators.note: to be in something is to be inside it

blocks.note: an el is an elevated railway line in American cities
the solver is 'you', and the old word for your is thy

explanation.surface: A solver queues to buy cleaning fluid.
explanation.walkthrough: Clues often address the solver as 'you', so solver's means your, here the archaic thy. 'Solvent' teases with 'Solver'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethyl, short for ethyl alcohol or ethyl acetate, names common chemical solvents used to dissolve other substances.

clue.text: Chess player heard to do what Humpty Dumpty did to friend — some egg!

indicators.note: something heard is taken in by the ear, so sound matters here rather than spelling

blocks.clueFragment: to do what Humpty Dumpty did
blocks.note: Humpty Dumpty had a great fall, and to fall over is to topple; the written form is spelt out by the words that follow
TO as written plus PAL, a friend; together they say the same thing
part of OVUM, Latin for egg

explanation.surface: A chess player is said to have pushed his pal off a wall, egg everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Veselin Topalov was world chess champion in 2005. The sound of 'topple' is spelt as 'to pal', confirmed by 'to friend'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bulgarian grandmaster held the world title, so he is a famous example of a top chess player.

clue.text: Moon-dweller's destination, largely mistaken, backed by German setter

indicators.note: largely means mostly, not entirely, so the end is cut off
something backed is moved in reverse, so it runs from end to start

blocks.note: WRONG without its last letter
the setter refers to themselves as I, which is ich in German

explanation.surface: An alien's travel plans are mostly wrong, according to a German puzzle-setter.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, the man in the moon came down too soon and asked his way to Norwich, an English cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme sends the man in the moon on his way to that East Anglian city, so it is where he was heading.

clue.text: Tin treated for corrosion awaiting maturity, perhaps

indicators.note: treated material has been processed and altered, so the letters come out changed

blocks.note: the three letters rearranged
rust is the corrosion of iron

explanation.surface: A tin can is treated to fight rust before it is ready.
explanation.walkthrough: Money left to a child is often held by trustees until the child comes of age; 'perhaps' flags that as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Assets kept by trustees for a beneficiary who is still a minor wait there until that heir comes of age.

clue.text: See 11
